claim: The CDK sensor consists of a fluorescently tagged CDK substrate that steadily translocates from the nucleus to the cytoplasm in response to increasing CDK activity and consequent sensor phosphorylation.
source: The CDK sensor consists of a fluorescently tagged CDK substrate that steadily translocates from the nucleus to the cytoplasm in response to increasing CDK activity and consequent sensor phosphorylation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of how the CDK sensor functions.

claim: The CDK sensor can distinguish cycling cells in G1 from quiescent cells in G0.
source: We show that the CDK sensor can distinguish cycling cells in G1 from quiescent cells in G0, revealing a possible commitment point and a cryptic stochasticity in an otherwise invariant C. elegans cell lineage.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: A predictive model of future proliferation behavior in C. elegans can be derived based on a snapshot of CDK activity in newly born cells.
source: Finally, we derive a predictive model of future proliferation behavior in C. elegans based on a snapshot of CDK activity in newly born cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through statistical modeling in the results section.

claim: Early embryos achieve rapid cell proliferation by omitting gap phases (G1 and G2) and establishing a biphasic cell cycle that rapidly alternates between DNA synthesis (S phase) and mitosis (M phase).
source: In early embryos, the emphasis is placed on rapid cell proliferation, which is achieved by omitting gap phases (G1 and G2) and establishing a biphasic cell cycle that rapidly alternates between DNA synthesis (S phase) and mitosis (M phase) (Edgar and O'Farrell, 1989; Newport and Kirschner, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: After several rounds of embryonic cell division, gap phases are introduced, coincident in many organisms with cell fate decisions and the execution of morphogenetic cell behaviors.
source: After several rounds of embryonic cell division, the gap phases are introduced, coincident in many organisms with cell fate decisions and the execution of morphogenetic cell behaviors (Foe, 1989; Grosshans and Wieschaus, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Gap phases are believed to function as commitment points for cell-cycle progression decisions.
source: These gap phases are believed to function as commitment points for cell-cycle progression decisions.
evidence: This represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The earliest point of commitment occurs during G1.
source: The earliest point of commitment occurs during G1, which is the focus of this study.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and the focus of the current study.

claim: Cells either engage in cell-cycle progression and enter S phase, or they exit the cell cycle altogether and enter a cell-cycle phase referred to as G0 and undergo quiescence or terminal differentiation.
source: Cells either engage in cell-cycle progression and enter S phase, or they exit the cell cycle altogether and enter a cell-cycle phase referred to as G0 and undergo quiescence or terminal differentiation (Sun and Buttitta, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The location of the G1 commitment point in yeast (Start) and cultured mammalian cells (Restriction Point) has in large part been spatiotemporally mapped and molecularly characterized.
source: Although the location of the G1 commitment point in yeast (Start) and cultured mammalian cells (Restriction Point) has in large part been spatiotemporally mapped and molecularly characterized (Hartwell et al., 1974; Pardee, 1974; Spencer et al., 2013), when cells make this decision in living organisms while integrating intrinsic and the extrinsic cues of their local microenvironment during development remains poorly understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: When cells make the G1 commitment decision in living organisms while integrating intrinsic and extrinsic cues of their local microenvironment during development remains poorly understood.
source: Although the location of the G1 commitment point in yeast (Start) and cultured mammalian cells (Restriction Point) has in large part been spatiotemporally mapped and molecularly characterized (Hartwell et al., 1974; Pardee, 1974; Spencer et al., 2013), when cells make this decision in living organisms while integrating intrinsic and the extrinsic cues of their local microenvironment during development remains poorly understood.
evidence: This represents a gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: In 2008, Sakaue-Sawano and colleagues engineered a multicolor fluorescent ubiquitination-based cell-cycle indicator (FUCCI) for mammalian cell culture.
source: In 2008, Sakaue-Sawano and colleagues engineered a multicolor fluorescent ubiquitination-based cell-cycle indicator (FUCCI) for mammalian cell culture (Sakaue-Sawano et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: FUCCI has since been adapted for many research organisms.
source: FUCCI has since been adapted for many research organisms (Özpolat et al., 2017; Zielke and Edgar, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FUCCI on its own cannot distinguish between a cell residing in G1 that will cycle again upon completing mitosis and a cell that is poised to enter G0.
source: However, FUCCI on its own cannot distinguish between a cell residing in G1 that will cycle again upon completing mitosis and a cell that is poised to enter G0 (Oki et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Hanh, Spencer and colleagues developed and implemented a single-color ratiometric sensor of cell-cycle state composed of a fragment of human DNA helicase B (DHB) fused to a fluorescent protein that is phosphorylated by CDKs.
source: To distinguish G1 from G0 in mammalian cell culture, Hanh, Spencer and colleagues developed and implemented a single-color ratiometric sensor of cell-cycle state composed of a fragment of human DNA helicase B (DHB) fused to a fluorescent protein that is phosphorylated by CDKs (Hahn et al., 2009; Schwarz et al., 2018; Spencer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Through quantitative measurements of CDK activity, the DHB sensor provided new insights into the proliferation-quiescence decision in cultured mammalian cells by identifying cycling cells that exit mitosis in a CDK-increasing (CDKinc) state and quiescent cells that exit mitosis in a CDK-low (CDKlow) state.
source: Notably, through quantitative measurements of CDK activity, this sensor provided new insights into the proliferation-quiescence decision in cultured mammalian cells by identifying cycling cells that exit mitosis in a CDK-increasing (CDKinc) state and quiescent cells that exit mitosis in a CDK-low (CDKlow) state (Spencer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A DHB-based CDK sensor has not been utilized to evaluate the proliferation-quiescence decision in vivo.
source: Nonetheless, a DHB-based CDK sensor has not been utilized to evaluate the proliferation-quiescence decision in vivo.
evidence: This represents a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: The study investigates the proliferation-quiescence decision in Caenorhabditis elegans and zebrafish.
source: In this study, we investigate the proliferation-quiescence decision in Caenorhabditis elegans and zebrafish, two powerful in vivo systems with radically different modes of development.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction.

claim: Transgenic CDK sensor lines were generated in C. elegans and zebrafish to examine the proliferation-quiescence decision live at mitotic exit.
source: We generate transgenic CDK sensor lines in each organism to examine this decision live at mitotic exit.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated throughout the results.

claim: By quantifying CDK activity, or DHB ratios, at mitotic exit, the study is able to predict future cell behavior across several embryonic and post-embryonic lineages.
source: By quantifying CDK activity, or DHB ratios, at mitotic exit, we are able to predict future cell behavior across several embryonic and post-embryonic lineages.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated in the results section.

claim: Cells generally exit mitosis with decreased CDK-activity levels.
source: Despite cells generally exiting mitosis with decreased CDK-activity levels, we reliably distinguish cycling cells that exit mitosis into G1, in a CDKinc state, from quiescent cells that exit mitosis into G0, in a CDKlow state.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The study reliably distinguishes cycling cells that exit mitosis into G1, in a CDKinc state, from quiescent cells that exit mitosis into G0, in a CDKlow state.
source: Despite cells generally exiting mitosis with decreased CDK-activity levels, we reliably distinguish cycling cells that exit mitosis into G1, in a CDKinc state, from quiescent cells that exit mitosis into G0, in a CDKlow state.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the introduction and demonstrated throughout the results.

claim: Endogenous CKI-1 levels are anti-correlated with CDK activity during the proliferation-quiescence decision.
source: To gain insights into cell-cycle progression commitment, we examine the activity of C. elegans cki-1, a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor (CKI) of the Cip/Kip family, demonstrating that endogenous CKI-1 levels are anti-correlated with CDK activity during the proliferation-quiescence decision.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated in the results section.

claim: Integration of CKI-1 levels in the mother cell and high CKI-1, low CDK activity at mitotic exit mediate the proliferation-quiescence decision.
source: We propose that integration of CKI-1 levels in the mother cell and high CKI-1, low CDK activity at mitotic exit mediate this decision.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The study uncovers a cryptic stochasticity that occurs in a temperature-dependent fashion in the C. elegans vulva.
source: By utilizing the CDK sensor to predict future cell behavior, we uncover a cryptic stochasticity that occurs in a temperature-dependent fashion in the C. elegans vulva, an otherwise invariant and well-characterized lineage.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated in the results section.

claim: Quiescent embryonic tissues in zebrafish display DHB ratios that correlate with those observed in G0 cells in C. elegans.
source: Finally, we reveal cell-cycle dynamics in zebrafish, an organism that lacks a defined cell lineage, demonstrating that quiescent embryonic tissues display DHB ratios that correlate with those observed in G0 cells in C. elegans.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated in the results section.

claim: A C. elegans codon-optimized fragment of human DHB composed of amino acids 994–1087 was synthesized.
source: We synthesized a C. elegans codon-optimized fragment of human DHB composed of amino acids 994–1087 (Hahn et al., 2009; Spencer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the design of the CDK sensor.

claim: The DHB fragment contains four serine residues that are consensus CDK phosphorylation sites.
source: The fragment contains four serine residues that are consensus CDK phosphorylation sites (Moser et al., 2018; Spencer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The serine residues in the DHB fragment flank a nuclear localization signal (NLS) that is adjacent to a nuclear export signal (NES).
source: These serines flank a nuclear localization signal (NLS) that is adjacent to a nuclear export signal (NES) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: When CDK activity is low, the NLS is strong, the NES is weak and DHB localizes to the nucleus.
source: When CDK activity is low, the NLS is strong, the NES is weak and DHB localizes to the nucleus.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: When CDK activity increases during cell-cycle entry, the NLS is masked and DHB re-localizes to the cytoplasm.
source: However, when CDK activity increases during cell-cycle entry, the NLS is masked and DHB re-localizes to the cytoplasm (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Two CDK sensors were generated by fusing green fluorescent protein (GFP) or two copies of a red fluorescent protein, mKate2 (2xmKate2), to the DHB C-terminus.
source: Using this DHB fragment, we generated two CDK sensors by fusing green fluorescent protein (GFP) or two copies of a red fluorescent protein, mKate2 (2xmKate2), to the DHB C-terminus (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: his-58/histone H2B fused to 2xmKate2 or GFP was co-expressed to visualize the nucleus, separated from DHB by a P2A self-cleaving viral peptide.
source: To visualize the nucleus, we co-expressed his-58/histone H2B fused to 2xmKate2 or GFP, respectively, which is separated from DHB by a P2A self-cleaving viral peptide (Ahier and Jarriault, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Expression of each CDK sensor was driven via a ubiquitous rps-27 promoter.
source: We drove the expression of each CDK sensor via a ubiquitous rps-27 promoter (Ruijtenberg and van den Heuvel, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: DHB::GFP localizes in a cell-cycle-dependent fashion during E16* star cell divisions, with DHB::GFP translocating from the nucleus to the cytoplasm and then re-locating to the nucleus at the completion of E16* star cell division.
source: To accomplish this, we tracked E16* star cell division from the E16–E20 stage and observed that DHB::GFP localizes in a cell-cycle-dependent fashion during these divisions, with DHB::GFP translocating from the nucleus to the cytoplasm and then re-locating to the nucleus at the completion of E16* star cell division (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DHB::2xmKate2 dynamically translocates from the nucleus to the cytoplasm during cell divisions in the early embryo.
source: Consistent with our observations using the GFP version of our CDK sensor in mid-embryogenesis, DHB::2xmKate2 also dynamically translocates from the nucleus to the cytoplasm during cell divisions in the early embryo (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A gradient of live CDK activity was detected in the adult C. elegans germline, from high in the distal mitotic progenitor zone to low in the proximal meiotic regions.
source: Here we detected a gradient of live CDK activity, from high in the distal mitotic progenitor zone to low in the proximal meiotic regions, as described with EdU incorporation and phospho-histone H3 staining (Kocsisova et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The CDK sensor is dynamic during cell-cycle progression in the C. elegans embryo and germline.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that our CDK sensor is dynamic during cell-cycle progression in the C. elegans embryo and germline.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented.

claim: All lineages examined (VPC, SM, and uterine) exhibited the same CDK sensor localization pattern during peak G2 (i.e. maximal nuclear exclusion).
source: All lineages exhibited the same CDK sensor localization pattern during peak G2 (i.e. maximal nuclear exclusion).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: RNAi depletion of cdk-1 induced a penetrant G2 phase arrest in the SM cells.
source: We then RNAi depleted the sole C. elegans CDK1 homolog, cdk-1, to induce a penetrant G2 phase arrest in the SM cells to corroborate these results.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I and J.

claim: Quantification of DHB ratios following cdk-1 RNAi treatment showed a mean ratio of 1.00 ± 0.28 and 2.36 ± 0.70 in the GFP and 2xmKate2 versions of the CDK sensor, respectively.
source: Quantification of DHB ratios following cdk-1 RNAi treatment showed a mean ratio of 1.00 ± 0.28 and 2.36 ± 0.70 in the GFP and 2xmKate2 versions of our CDK sensor, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I and J).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I and J.

claim: In G1, DHB::GFP and DHB::2xmKate2 were nuclear localized after mitotic exit with mean ratios of 0.35 ± 0.14 and 0.58 ± 0.32 in VPCs, 0.59 ± 0.11 and 0.97 ± 0.20 in SMs, and 0.67 ± 0.10 and 1.13 ± 0.17 in uterine cells.
source: In G1, DHB::GFP and DHB::2xmKate2 were nuclear localized after mitotic exit with mean ratios of 0.35 ± 0.14 and 0.58 ± 0.32 in VPCs, 0.59 ± 0.11 and 0.97 ± 0.20 in SMs, and 0.67 ± 0.10 and 1.13 ± 0.17 in uterine cells (Figure 1G and H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Punctate expression of PCN-1::GFP correlated with mean DHB::2xmKate2 ratios of 1.02 ± 0.22 in VPC, 0.89 ± 0.16 in SM, and 1.00 ± 0.10 in uterine lineages.
source: Analysis of time-lapse data found that punctate expression of PCN-1::GFP correlated with mean DHB::2xmKate2 ratios of 1.02 ± 0.22 in VPC (Figure 1I and J), 0.89 ± 0.16 in SM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K and M; Figure 1—video 2), and 1.00 ± 0.10 in uterine (Figure 1—figure supplement 1L and M) lineages.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: DHB ratios can be established for each interphase state (G1/S/G2) across several post-embryonic somatic lineages using the CDK sensor paired with a PCNA reporter.
source: Despite individual lineages showing differences in CDK activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and M–O), primarily in G1, we can establish DHB ratios for each interphase state (G1/S/G2) across several post-embryonic somatic lineages using our CDK sensor paired with a PCNA reporter.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented.

claim: In asynchronously dividing MCF10A epithelial cell lines, cells that exited mitosis into a CDK2low state had a high probability of staying in G0 compared to cells that exited at a CDK2inc state.
source: In asynchronously dividing MCF10A epithelial cell lines, cells that exited mitosis into a CDK2low state had a high probability of staying in G0 compared to cells that exited at a CDK2inc state (Spencer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The SM cells undergo three rounds of cell division during the L3 and L4 larval stages before exiting the cell cycle and differentiating into uterine muscle (um) and vulval muscle (vm).
source: The SM cells undergo three rounds of cell division during the L3 and L4 larval stages before exiting the cell cycle and differentiating into uterine muscle (um) and vulval muscle (vm) (Figure 2A; Sulston and Horvitz, 1977).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Shortly after the first and second SM cell divisions, CDK activity increases immediately after mitotic exit from an intermediate level, designated as a CDKinc state.
source: Quantification of DHB::GFP in this lineage revealed that shortly after the first and second divisions, CDK activity increases immediately after mitotic exit from an intermediate level, which we designate as a CDKinc state (Figure 2B and C; Figure 2—video 1)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: CDK activity following the third and terminal SM cell division remains low, designated as a CDKlow state.
source: Conversely, CDK activity following the third and terminal division remains low, which we designate as a CDKlow state.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Bootstrap analyses support a significant difference in DHB::GFP ratios between pre-terminal (CDKinc) and terminal divisions (CDKlow) in SM cells, but not among pre-terminal divisions.
source: Bootstrap analyses support a significant difference in DHB::GFP ratios between pre-terminal (CDKinc) and terminal divisions (CDKlow), but not among pre-terminal divisions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: VU and SS cells undergo several rounds of division during the L3 larval stage and exit the cell cycle in the early L4 stage.
source: VU and SS cells undergo several rounds of division during the L3 larval stage and exit the cell cycle in the early L4 stage (Figure 2D; Sulston and Horvitz, 1977).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Both VU and SS somatic gonad lineages exit the round of cell division prior to their final division into a CDKinc state and then exit into a CDKlow state following their terminal division.
source: Similar to the SM lineage, both somatic gonad lineages exit the round of cell division prior to their final division into a CDKinc state and then exit into a CDKlow state following their terminal division (Figure 2E and F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F; Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Bootstrap analyses support a significant difference between DHB::GFP ratios in pre-terminal versus terminal divisions in the developing somatic gonad.
source: Bootstrap analyses also support a significant difference between DHB::GFP ratios in pre-terminal versus terminal divisions in the developing somatic gonad (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Induced expression of CKI-1 resulted in SM and uterine cells entering a CDKlow G0 state, with mean DHB ratios of 0.10 ± 0.05 and 0.12 ± 0.05, respectively.
source: Indeed, in the SM and uterine lineages, induced expression of CKI-1 resulted in cells entering a CDKlow G0 state, with mean DHB ratios of 0.10 ± 0.05 and 0.12 ± 0.05, respectively (Figure 2G), as compared to control animals that lacked heat shock-induced expression (SM: 0.99 ± 0.82, uterine: 0.71 ± 0.35) or lacked the inducible transgene (SM: 0.96 ± 0.77, uterine: 1.00 ± 0.37).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Induced G0 arrest by ectopic expression of CKI-1 is functionally equivalent, by CDK-activity levels, to the G0 arrest that occurs following mitotic exit in an unperturbed cell destined to undergo quiescence.
source: Thus, induced G0 arrest by ectopic expression of CKI-1 is functionally equivalent, by CDK-activity levels, to the G0 arrest that occurs following mitotic exit in an unperturbed cell destined to undergo quiescence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The C. elegans vulva is derived from three cells (P5.p–P7.p), which undergo three rounds of cell division during the L3 and early L4 larval stages.
source: The C. elegans vulva is derived from three cells (P5.p–P7.p), which undergo three rounds of cell division during the L3 and early L4 larval stages (Figure 3A and B; Katz et al., 1995; Sternberg and Horvitz, 1986; Sulston and Horvitz, 1977).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The two D cells, the innermost granddaughters of the 2°-fated P5.p and P7.p, exit the cell cycle one round early, resulting in a total of 22 cells that comprise the adult vulva.
source: Rather than giving rise to 24 cells, the two D cells, the innermost granddaughters of the 2°-fated P5.p and P7.p, exit the cell cycle one round early. This results in a total of 22 cells, which comprise the adult vulva (Katz et al., 1995; Sulston and Horvitz, 1977).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations.

claim: The daughters of P5.p–P7.p all exited their first division into a CDKinc state.
source: The daughters of P5.p–P7.p all exited their first division into a CDKinc state (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The D cell exited into and remained in a CDKlow state, while the remaining VPCs exited into a CDKinc state and continued to progress through the cell cycle.
source: The D cell exited into and remained in a CDKlow state, while the remaining VPCs exited into a CDKinc state and continued to progress through the cell cycle (Figure 3C and D; Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: All remaining VPCs exited into a CDKlow state at their terminal division.
source: All remaining VPCs exited into a CDKlow state at their terminal division.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Bootstrap analyses support the ability to quantitatively distinguish between a cell that has completed mitosis and will continue to cycle (CDKinc) from a cell that exits mitosis and enters a G0 state (CDKlow).
source: Consistent with these results, bootstrap analyses (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–G) support our qualitative results, such that we can quantitatively distinguish between a cell that has completed mitosis and will continue to cycle (CDKinc) from a cell that exits mitosis and enters a G0 state (CDKlow).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–G.

claim: In mammalian cell culture, endogenous levels of p21Cip1 during G2 are predictive of whether a cell will go on to divide or enter quiescence, senescence, or terminal differentiation.
source: In mammalian cell culture, endogenous levels of p21Cip1 during G2 are predictive of whether a cell will go on to divide or enter quiescence, senescence, or terminal differentiation (Hsu et al., 2019; Moser et al., 2018; Overton et al., 2014; Spencer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Generally low levels of GFP::CKI-1 were detected at the Pn.p 2 cell stage.
source: We detected generally low levels of GFP::CKI-1 at the Pn.p 2 cell stage (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: At the Pn.p 4 cell stage, an increase in GFP::CKI-1 levels was detected in cycling cells prior to their next cell division, peaking in G2.
source: In their daughter cells, at the Pn.p 4 cell stage, we detected an increase in GFP::CKI-1 levels in cycling cells prior to their next cell division, peaking in G2 (Figure 4A, B and D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The D cell, which becomes post-mitotic after the Pn.p 4 cell stage division, exits mitosis with higher levels of GFP::CKI-1 than its CD mother.
source: Notably, the D cell, which becomes post-mitotic after this cell division, exits mitosis with higher levels of GFP::CKI-1 than its CD mother (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The remaining VPCs at the Pn.p 6 cell and 8 cell stage show high levels of GFP::CKI-1 that peak immediately after mitotic exit and remain high during the post-mitotic L4 stage.
source: This trend holds true for the remaining VPCs at the Pn.p 6 cell and 8 cell stage, which show high levels of GFP::CKI-1 that peak immediately after mitotic exit and remain high during the post-mitotic L4 stage (Figure 4A, B, E and F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Increasing levels of GFP::CKI-1 in the G2 phase of mother cells peak in their quiescent daughter cells in the uterine and SM cell lineages.
source: We also observed increasing levels of GFP::CKI-1 in the G2 phase of mother cells that peak in their quiescent daughter cells in the uterine (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and SM cell lineages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Levels of GFP::CKI-1 increase in mother cells and remain high upon mitotic exit in daughter cells with CDKlow activity.
source: Thus, levels of GFP::CKI-1 increase in mother cells and remain high upon mitotic exit in daughter cells with CDKlow activity.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data.

claim: The proliferation-quiescence decision is already underway in the G2 phase of the previous cell cycle and correlates with CKI-1 levels in the mother cell.
source: These results suggest that the proliferation-quiescence decision is already underway in the G2 phase of the previous cell cycle and correlates with CKI-1 levels in the mother cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Many cells appeared to bypass their final division and undergo early cell-cycle quiescence with coincident high levels of GFP::CKI-1 and low DHB ratios.
source: In particular, we noted that many cells appeared to bypass their final division and undergo early cell-cycle quiescence with coincident high levels of GFP::CKI-1 and low DHB ratios.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an observation.

claim: The GFP::CKI-1 line could be behaving as a gain-of-function mutant, as GFP insertions at the N-terminus could interfere with proteasome-mediated protein degradation of CKI-1.
source: We hypothesized that the line we generated could be behaving as a gain-of-function mutant, as GFP insertions at the N-terminus could interfere with proteasome-mediated protein degradation of CKI-1 (Bloom et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the text with a citation.

claim: Heat shock-induced CKI-1 expression uniformly drove VPCs at the Pn.p 2 cell stage into a CDKlow G0 state with mean DHB ratios of 0.11 ± 0.05.
source: Consistent with our finding that high levels of endogenous GFP::CKI-1 can lead to early cell-cycle quiescence, heat shock-induced CKI-1 expression uniformly drove VPCs at the Pn.p 2 cell stage into a CDKlow G0 state with mean DHB ratios of 0.11 ± 0.05 (Figure 4I), as compared to control animals that lacked heat shock-induced expression (0.46 ± 0.87) or lacked the inducible cki-1 transgene (0.47 ± 0.42).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Most of the VPCs of heat shocked larvae that were allowed to recover for 5 hr remained quiescent (0.35 ± 0.29).
source: Strikingly, most of the VPCs of heat shocked larvae that were allowed to recover for 5 hr remained quiescent (0.35 ± 0.29) (Figure 4I), as VPCs that received an effective pulse of CKI-1 failed to divide again.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4I.

claim: An average of 6.86 VPCs were present hours later at the L4 stage in heat shocked animals as opposed to the wild type vulva composed of 22 total cells.
source: We observed an average of 6.86 VPCs present hours later at the L4 stage as opposed to the wild type vulva composed of 22 total cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Cycling cells are highly sensitive to levels of CKIs and increased expression can induce a G0 state.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that cycling cells are highly sensitive to levels of CKIs and that increased expression can induce a G0 state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: At high temperatures it has been observed that the D cell, the inner-most granddaughter of P5.p or P7.p, will go on to divide.
source: However, at high temperatures it has been observed that the D cell, the inner-most granddaughter of P5.p or P7.p, will go on to divide (Figure 5A; Sternberg, 1984; Sternberg and Horvitz, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A rare occurrence of D cells expressing elevated DHB ratios was noticed during time-lapse analysis of VPC divisions captured under standard laboratory conditions.
source: Unexpectedly, we noticed a rare occurrence of D cells expressing elevated DHB ratios during the course of time-lapse analysis of VPC divisions captured under standard laboratory conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an observation.

claim: In both CDK sensor strains grown at 25°C, a cycling D cell was observed with a 4–6% penetrance.
source: To determine the penetrance of the cycling D cell phenotype, we inspected each of our CDK sensor lines grown at 25°C, a high temperature that is still within normal range for C. elegans. In both strains we observed a cycling D cell with a 4–6% penetrance (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At 25°C, a low penetrance (2%) of cycling D cells was observed in a strain expressing an endogenously tagged DNA licensing factor, CDT-1::GFP.
source: At 25°C, we observed a low penetrance (2%) of cycling D cells in a strain expressing an endogenously tagged DNA licensing factor, CDT-1::GFP (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), which is cytosolic in cycling cells (Matus et al., 2014; Matus et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: L2 larvae expressing a seam cell reporter that were temperature shifted from 20°C to 28°C displayed approximately a 30% occurrence of extra D cell divisions.
source: From lineage analysis, L2 larvae, expressing a seam cell reporter (scm>GFP), that were temperature shifted from 20°C to 28°C displayed approximately a 30% occurrence of extra D cell divisions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: In all 10 cases where D cells were born into a CDKinc state, the CDKinc D cell went on to divide.
source: These time-lapses revealed 10 occurrences of D cells born into a CDKinc rather than a CDKlow state (Figure 5C and D; Figure 5—video 1). In all 10 cases, the CDKinc D cell goes on to divide (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: CDK activity shortly after mitosis is a predictor of future cell behavior, even in rare stochastic cases of extra cell divisions in C. elegans.
source: Thus, we find that CDK activity shortly after mitosis is a predictor of future cell behavior, even in rare stochastic cases of extra cell divisions in C. elegans, an organism with a well-defined cell lineage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Two CDK sensor lines with different fluorescent protein combinations were generated in zebrafish: DHB-mNeonGreen (DHB-mNG) and DHB-mScarlet (DHB-mSc) with H2B-mSc and H2B-miRFP670, respectively.
source: To investigate the predictive capability of DHB ratios in zebrafish, we generated two CDK sensor lines with different fluorescent protein combinations, DHB-mNeonGreen (DHB-mNG) and DHB-mScarlet (DHB-mSc) with H2B-mSc and H2B-miRFP670, respectively, to allow for flexibility with imaging and experimental design (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Both zebrafish transgenes are under the control of the hsp70l heat shock-inducible promoter, which produces robust ubiquitous expression after shifting the temperature from 28.5 to 40°C for 30 min.
source: Both transgenes are under the control of the hsp70l heat shock-inducible promoter, which produces robust ubiquitous expression after shifting the temperature from 28.5 to 40°C for 30 min (Figure 6B; Halloran et al., 2000; Shoji et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A transgenic line, Tg(ubb:Lck-mNG), was generated that ubiquitously labels the plasma membrane with mNG.
source: We also generated a transgenic line, Tg(ubb:Lck-mNG), that ubiquitously labels the plasma membrane with mNG, which we crossed into the HS:DHB-mSc-2A-H2B-miRFP670 line to simultaneously visualize CDK activity (DHB-mSc), segment nuclei (H2B-miRFP670) and segment the plasma membrane (LCK-mNG) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: DHB localizes in a cell-cycle-dependent manner in both zebrafish CDK sensor lines.
source: To verify that DHB localizes in a cell-cycle-dependent manner in both CDK sensor lines, we first used time-lapse microscopy and quantified DHB ratios across cell divisions in the tailbud of bud or 22 somite-stage embryos (Figure 6C and D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: In zebrafish, maximal nuclear exclusion of the CDK sensor occurs shortly before mitosis in G2 with ratios of 3.42 ± 0.56 (DHB-mNG) and 6.57 ± 2.00 (DHB-mSc).
source: We observed the expected localization pattern for both CDK sensor lines, with maximal nuclear exclusion of the sensor shortly before mitosis in G2 (3.42 ± 0.56 (DHB-mNG) and 6.57 ± 2.00 (DHB-mSc)) and low ratios (0.69 ± 0.17 (DHB-mNG) and 0.51 ± 0.21 (DHB-mSC)) representing nuclear accumulation of the sensor shortly after mitosis in G1 (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: In zebrafish, low DHB ratios of 0.69 ± 0.17 (DHB-mNG) and 0.51 ± 0.21 (DHB-mSC) represent nuclear accumulation of the sensor shortly after mitosis in G1.
source: We observed the expected localization pattern for both CDK sensor lines, with maximal nuclear exclusion of the sensor shortly before mitosis in G2 (3.42 ± 0.56 (DHB-mNG) and 6.57 ± 2.00 (DHB-mSc)) and low ratios (0.69 ± 0.17 (DHB-mNG) and 0.51 ± 0.21 (DHB-mSC)) representing nuclear accumulation of the sensor shortly after mitosis in G1 (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Approximately 38.5 min after PCNA puncta formation in zebrafish, corresponding to mid-S phase, the DHB ratio is 1.36 ± 0.36, which is significantly higher than the G1 DHB value (0.51 ± 0.21).
source: Approximately 38.5 min after puncta formation, corresponding to mid-S phase, the DHB ratio is 1.36 ± 0.36, which is significantly higher than the G1 DHB value (0.51 ± 0.21; Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Both zebrafish CDK sensor lines localize in a cell-cycle-dependent fashion, and quantitative measurements can be used to determine interphase states.
source: Thus, we conclude that both CDK sensor lines localize in a cell-cycle-dependent fashion, and that quantitative measurements can be used to determine interphase states.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Imaging of the developing zebrafish tailbud revealed cells in all phases of the cell cycle with mean DHB ratios of 1.95 ± 1.74 (mNG) and 1.67 ± 2.05 (mSC).
source: Imaging of the developing tailbud revealed cells in all phases of the cell cycle with mean DHB ratios of 1.95 ± 1.74 (mNG) and 1.67 ± 2.05 (mSC) (Figure 7A and B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs) in the zebrafish tailbud have been reported to be predominantly arrested in the G2 phase of the cell cycle.
source: The tailbud of vertebrate embryos contain neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs) (Martin, 2016), which in zebrafish have been reported to be predominantly arrested in the G2 phase of the cell cycle (Bouldin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cells with high CDK activity were observed in the zebrafish tailbud, consistent with G2 arrest.
source: Consistent with this, we observed cells with high CDK activity in the tailbud (orange arrows; Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Treatment with the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib eliminated the enrichment of high CDK activity cells in the zebrafish tailbud, leading to a significant increase of cells with low CDK activity (0.58 ± 0.3).
source: This enrichment is eliminated when embryos are treated with the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib, leading to a significant increase of cells in the tailbud with low CDK activity (0.58 ± 0.3), similar in range to the G1/G0 values we measured during time-lapse (0.69 ± 0.17; Figure 7C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7C–D.

claim: Primitive red blood cells in the intermediate cell mass of 24 hpf zebrafish embryos display high CDK activity (3.00 ± 0.97) indicating that they are likely in the G2 phase of the cell cycle.
source: We also made the surprising observation that primitive red blood cells in the intermediate cell mass of 24 hr post-fertilization (hpf) embryos, which are nucleated in zebrafish, display high CDK activity (3.00 ± 0.97) indicating that they are likely in the G2 phase of the cell cycle (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and F), suggesting that cell-cycle regulation may be important for hematopoiesis (Brönnimann et al., 2018; De La Garza et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Adaxial cells in zebrafish are the slow muscle precursors and are considered to be in a quiescent state through the cooperative action of Cdkn1ca (p57) and MyoD.
source: The adaxial cells are the slow muscle precursors and are considered to be in a quiescent state through the cooperative action of Cdkn1ca (p57) and MyoD (Osborn et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the most recently formed somites at 24 hpf in zebrafish, cells can be observed in all phases of the cell cycle.
source: In the most recently formed somites at 24 hpf, cells can be observed in all phases of the cell cycle (Figure 7F and K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7F and K.

claim: Treatment with palbociclib caused zebrafish somite cells to arrest with low CDK activity in G1/G0 (0.33 ± 0.42).
source: Consistent with what we observed in the tailbud, treatment with palbociclib also caused somite cells to arrest with low CDK activity in G1/G0 (0.33 ± 0.42; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: Adaxial cells in zebrafish possess low CDK activity (0.13 ± 0.04).
source: As opposed to the majority of cells in the lateral regions of recently formed somites, adaxial cells possess low CDK activity (0.13 ± 0.04; Figure 7K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7K.

claim: At later stages, the majority of cells in the lateral regions of the zebrafish somite will differentiate into fast skeletal muscles fibers, which are considered to be in a quiescent state.
source: At later stages, the majority of cells in the lateral regions of the somite will differentiate into fast skeletal muscles fibers, which are also considered to be in a quiescent state (Halevy et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Examination of DHB ratios in 72 hpf zebrafish skeletal muscle fibers revealed they have low CDK activity (0.14 ± 0.04 (mNG) and 0.13 ± 0.04 (mSc)), similar to the adaxial cells, but significantly different than the mean DHB ratios of undifferentiated cells at 24 hr (0.82 ± 0.70 (mNG) and 0.99 ± 0.084 (mSc)).
source: Examination of DHB ratios in 72 hpf skeletal muscle fibers revealed they have low CDK activity (0.14 ± 0.04 (mNG) and 0.13 ± 0.04 (mSc)), similar to the adaxial cells, but significantly different than the mean DHB ratios of undifferentiated cells at 24 hr (0.82 ± 0.70 (mNG) and 0.99 ± 0.084 (mSc); Figure 7H and K, Figure 7—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: From static imaging in zebrafish, cell types with low CDK activity that are thought to be quiescent can be identified.
source: Thus, from our static imaging, we can identify cell types with low CDK activity that are thought to be quiescent.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Notochord progenitor cells in zebrafish are held transiently in G1/G0 before re-entering the cell cycle upon joining the notochord.
source: We compared adaxial cells to notochord progenitor cells, which are held transiently in G1/G0 before re-entering the cell cycle upon joining the notochord (Figure 7I; Sugiyama et al., 2014; Sugiyama et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and shown in Figure 7I.

claim: The mean DHB-mNG ratio of the zebrafish notochord progenitors (0.32 ± 0.08) is significantly higher than the DHB-mNG ratio of the quiescent adaxial cells (0.13 ± 0.04).
source: Notably, the mean DHB-mNG ratio of the notochord progenitors (0.32 ± 0.08) is significantly higher than the DHB-mNG ratio of the quiescent adaxial cells (0.13 ± 0.04; Figure 7F and J).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7F and J.

claim: The elevated DHB ratio in zebrafish notochord progenitors is consistent at two other earlier developmental stages, 90% epiboly (0.28 ± 0.08) and 18 somites (0.27 ± 0.09).
source: This elevated DHB ratio is consistent in notochord progenitors at two other earlier developmental stages, 90% epiboly (0.28 ± 0.08) and 18 somites (0.27 ± 0.09; Figure 7K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7K.

claim: The mean DHB-mSc ratio in the zebrafish notochord progenitors (0.33 ± 0.08) is significantly different than the differentiated epidermis (0.13 ± 0.03).
source: The mean DHB-mSc ratio in the notochord progenitors (0.33 ± 0.08) is also significantly different than the differentiated epidermis (0.13 ± 0.03; Figure 7J, Figure 7—figure supplement 1K–L).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Based on the difference in DHB ratios between notochord progenitors and differentiated cell types in zebrafish, the CDK sensor can infer cell cycle state and distinguish between a cycling G1 state and a quiescent G0 state.
source: Based on this difference in DHB ratios between notochord progenitors and differentiated cell types, including muscle and epidermis (Figure 7K), and our knowledge of the normal biology of these cells, we conclude that the CDK sensor can infer cell cycle state in the zebrafish, as it can distinguish between a cycling G1 state and a quiescent G0 state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and knowledge of cell biology.

claim: Plotting of all CDK sensor trace data in C. elegans, irrespective of lineage, demonstrated that cells entering a CDKlow state after mitosis corresponded to quiescent cells, while cells that exited mitosis into a CDKinc state corresponded to cells from pre-terminal divisions.
source: For C. elegans, plotting of all CDK sensor trace data, irrespective of lineage, demonstrated that cells entering a CDKlow state after mitosis corresponded to quiescent cells, while cells that exited mitosis into a CDKinc state corresponded to cells from pre-terminal divisions.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: In zebrafish, traces from the tailbud could be classified into CDKlow and CDKinc populations.
source: For zebrafish, in a lineage agnostic manner, we plotted all the traces from the tailbud. We classified cells as CDKlow that remained below 0.19, the upper bound of the DHB ratio for quiescent adaxial cells at this stage of development (Figure 7K), for three or more frames post-anaphase. Indeed, we found that these traces could also be classified into CDKlow and CDKinc populations (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8C.

claim: In zebrafish, in addition to a fast cycling population of cells, cells that maintain a CDKinc DHB ratio but appear to stay in a prolonged G1 phase were identified, potentially representing a slow cycling population of cells.
source: In addition to a fast cycling population of cells at this developmental stage, we also identified cells that maintain a CDKinc DHB ratio but appear to stay in a prolonged G1 phase, potentially representing a slow cycling population of cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8C.

claim: A classifier trained on post-anaphase CDK activity in C. elegans VPC trace data correctly predicted cell fate 92% (n = 24/26 single-cell traces) of the time, including the two occurrences of a stochastic mitotic D cell in the data set.
source: To test the predictive power of the classifier, we analyzed CDK trace data from the births of C and D cells, where some D cells stochastically divide (Figure 5). Our classifier correctly predicted cell fate 92% (n = 24/26 single-cell traces) of the time, including the two occurrences of a stochastic mitotic D cell in the data set (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8D.

claim: A cell-type agnostic classifier trained using 75% of all collected C. elegans time-lapse trace data correctly predicted the difference between a CDKinc proliferative cell and a CDKlow quiescent cell 93% (62/67) of the time.
source: Finally, to determine whether we could predict future cell behavior independent of cell type, we trained a new classifier using 75% of all collected C. elegans time-lapse trace data from the SM, uterine, and VPC lineages. We used the remaining 25% of traces as test data. When cross-referenced with the known C. elegans lineage, our cell-type agnostic classifier correctly predicted the difference between a CDKinc proliferative cell and a CDKlow quiescent cell 93% (62/67) of the time.
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: During development, cycling cells encounter a bifurcation in CDK activity following mitosis where they either increase in CDK activity and become poised to cycle, or exit into a CDKlow state and undergo cell-cycle quiescence.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that during development, cycling cells encounter a bifurcation in CDK activity following mitosis where they either: (1) increase in CDK activity and become poised to cycle, or (2) exit into a CDKlow state and undergo cell-cycle quiescence (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Cells from developing tissue in C. elegans and zebrafish must cross an early commitment point in the cell cycle where these cells must make the decision to divide or enter G0.
source: Thus, we suggest a model where cells from developing tissue in C. elegans and zebrafish must cross an early commitment point in the cell cycle where these cells must make the decision to divide or enter G0.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data and shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The decision to undergo quiescence is crucial to tissue integration and organization and is in part likely controlled by the activity of evolutionarily conserved CKI(s) in the mother cell that control daughter cell CDK activity.
source: The decision to undergo quiescence is crucial to tissue integration and organization and is in part likely controlled by the activity of evolutionarily conserved CKI(s) in the mother cell that control daughter cell CDK activity (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data and shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The DHB transgenic lines generated in this study will allow researchers to distinguish G1 from G0 shortly after a cell has divided and directly study G0-related cell behaviors, such as quiescence, terminal differentiation, and senescence, in living organisms.
source: The DHB transgenic lines generated in this study will allow researchers to distinguish G1 from G0 shortly after a cell has divided and directly study G0-related cell behaviors, such as quiescence, terminal differentiation, and senescence, in living organisms.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion about the utility of the tool.

claim: CDK sensors have been used to distinguish between proliferative and quiescent cells in asynchronous mammalian cell culture populations.
source: Previously, CDK sensors have been used to distinguish between proliferative and quiescent cells in asynchronous mammalian cell culture populations (Arora et al., 2017; Cappell et al., 2016; Gast et al., 2018; Gookin et al., 2017; Miller et al., 2018; Moser et al., 2018; Overton et al., 2014; Spencer et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: As mammalian cells complete mitosis, they are born into either a CDK2inc state in which they are more likely to divide again or a CDK2low state in which they remain quiescent.
source: As mammalian cells complete mitosis, they are born into either a CDK2inc state in which they are more likely to divide again or a CDK2low state in which they remain quiescent.
evidence: This represents established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: In C. elegans, CDKinc and CDKlow states precisely correlate with the lineage pattern of the three post-embryonic tissues examined: the SM cells, uterine cells, and VPCs.
source: Strikingly, in C. elegans these states precisely correlate with the lineage pattern of the three post-embryonic tissues we examined: the SM cells, uterine cells, and VPCs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Cells born into a CDKinc state in C. elegans represented pre-terminal divisions, whereas cells born into a CDKlow state were quiescent and represented cells that had undergone their terminal division.
source: Cells born into a CDKinc state represented pre-terminal divisions, whereas cells born into a CDKlow state were quiescent and represented cells that had undergone their terminal division.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: By distinguishing CDKinc and CDKlow states, a rare stochasticity first described nearly 36 years ago in the C. elegans vulval lineage was accurately identified shortly after cell birth.
source: By distinguishing these two states in CDK activity, we were able to accurately identify shortly after cell birth a rare stochasticity that was first described through careful end-point lineage analysis nearly 36 years ago in the C. elegans vulval lineage (Sternberg, 1984; Sternberg and Horvitz, 1986).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous literature.

claim: Statistical modeling demonstrated that future cell behavior in C. elegans could be predicted with >85% accuracy just 20 min post-anaphase.
source: Further, statistical modeling demonstrated that we could predict future cell behavior with >85% accuracy in C. elegans just 20 min post-anaphase.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: From static imaging in zebrafish, CDKinc cells in G1, such as notochord progenitors, which re-enter the cell cycle after joining the notochord, could be readily distinguished from quiescent tissues that contain CDKlow cells in G0, such as skeletal muscle and epidermis.
source: From static imaging in zebrafish, we found that we could readily distinguish between CDKinc cells in G1, such as notochord progenitors, which re-enter the cell cycle after joining the notochord, and quiescent tissues that contain CDKlow cells in G0, such as skeletal muscle and epidermis.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The classic model of the Restriction Point is that mammalian cells are born uncommitted and that the cell-cycle progression decision is not made until several hours after mitosis.
source: The classic model of the Restriction Point, the point in G1 at which cells in culture decide to commit to the cell cycle and no longer require growth factors (e.g. mitogens), is that mammalian cells are born uncommitted and that the cell-cycle progression decision is not made until several hours after mitosis (Jones and Kazlauskas, 2001; Pardee, 1974; Zetterberg and Larsson, 1985; Zwang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: An alternative model proposes that during the G2 phase of the cell cycle, the mother cell is influenced by levels of p21 and cyclin D and these levels affect the phosphorylation status of Rb in CDKlow and CDKinc daughter cells, respectively.
source: An alternative model has been proposed in studies using single-cell measurements of CDK2 activity in asynchronous populations of MCF10A cells (Spencer et al., 2013) and other nontumorigenic as well as tumorigenic cell lines (Moser et al., 2018). This model extends the classic Restriction Point model for cell cycle commitment. During the G2 phase of the cell cycle, the mother cell is influenced by levels of p21 and cyclin D and these levels affect the phosphorylation status of Rb in CDKlow and CDKinc daughter cells, respectively (Min et al., 2020; Moser et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In CDKlow daughter cells, phospho-Rb is low, and these cells are still sensitive to mitogens.
source: In CDKlow daughter cells, phospho-Rb is low, and these cells are still sensitive to mitogens.
evidence: This represents knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Mother cells whose daughters are born into a CDKinc G1 state will divide again, expressing low levels of GFP::CKI-1.
source: Similar to in vitro experiments (Moser et al., 2018; Spencer et al., 2013), we found that mother cells whose daughters are born into a CDKinc G1 state will divide again, expressing low levels of GFP::CKI-1.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings with citations to previous literature.

claim: Mother cells of daughters that will exit the cell cycle express a peak of GFP::CKI-1 in G2 which increases as daughter cells are born into a CDKlow G0 state.
source: In contrast, mother cells of daughters that will exit the cell cycle express a peak of GFP::CKI-1 in G2 which increases as daughter cells are born into a CDKlow G0 state.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The data demonstrate that an extended Restriction Point exists in the cell cycle of intact Metazoa.
source: Thus, our data demonstrate that an extended Restriction Point exists in the cell cycle of intact Metazoa.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The in vivo proliferation-quiescence decision can be predicted in C. elegans by CDK activity shortly after mitotic exit and is highly sensitive to levels of CKI-1 shortly before and after the mother cell divides.
source: Furthermore, the in vivo proliferation-quiescence decision can be predicted in C. elegans by CDK activity shortly after mitotic exit and, based on our gain-of-function studies, is highly sensitive to levels of CKI-1 shortly before and after the mother cell divides.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The CDK sensor functions in both C. elegans and zebrafish to read out cell cycle state dynamically, and unlike other in vivo cell-cycle sensors, can distinguish between proliferative and quiescent cells within an hour of cell birth.
source: We demonstrate here that the CDK sensor functions in both C. elegans and zebrafish to read out cell cycle state dynamically, and unlike other in vivo cell-cycle sensors, can distinguish between proliferative and quiescent cells within an hour of cell birth.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion.

claim: As nematodes and vertebrates last shared a common ancestor over 500 million years ago, the CDK sensor is likely to function in a similar fashion across Metazoa.
source: As nematodes and vertebrates last shared a common ancestor over 500 million years ago, this suggests that the CDK sensor is likely to function in a similar fashion across Metazoa.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary relationships.

claim: The broad functionality of the CDK sensor will offer researchers a unique opportunity to dissect the relationship between cell cycle state and cell fate during normal development, cellular reprogramming, and tissue regeneration.
source: The broad functionality of the sensor will offer researchers a unique opportunity to dissect the relationship between cell cycle state and cell fate during normal development, cellular reprogramming, and tissue regeneration.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential applications of the tool.

claim: An increasing body of evidence suggests that cell cycle state impinges on morphogenetic events ranging from gastrulation, convergent extension and cellular invasion.
source: Finally, as an increasing body of evidence suggests that cell cycle state impinges on morphogenetic events ranging from gastrulation (Grosshans and Wieschaus, 2000; Murakami et al., 2004), convergent extension (Leise and Mueller, 2004) and cellular invasion (Kohrman and Matus, 2017; Matus et al., 2015; Medwig-Kinney et al., 2020), this CDK sensor will provide the means to increase our understanding of the relationship between interphase states and morphogenesis during normal development and diseases arising from cell-cycle defects, such as cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The CDK sensor will provide the means to increase understanding of the relationship between interphase states and morphogenesis during normal development and diseases arising from cell-cycle defects, such as cancer.
source: Finally, as an increasing body of evidence suggests that cell cycle state impinges on morphogenetic events ranging from gastrulation (Grosshans and Wieschaus, 2000; Murakami et al., 2004), convergent extension (Leise and Mueller, 2004) and cellular invasion (Kohrman and Matus, 2017; Matus et al., 2015; Medwig-Kinney et al., 2020), this CDK sensor will provide the means to increase our understanding of the relationship between interphase states and morphogenesis during normal development and diseases arising from cell-cycle defects, such as cancer.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential applications of the tool.
